kicker: Hotrod Outdoor Alaska Fishing · round report
title: Asset Quality Round Two
lede: The weakest assets rebuilt: all 32 animals and birds as smooth shapes with their markings, birds that fold their wings at rest and stretch their necks out in flight, rounder birch, aspen and poplar crowns, far mountains without blocky shading, and campfires with stones, ash and split logs. Against the previous build, over eight places: 6.4% fewer draw calls and 4.4% more triangles, the same textures and one more shader program. Timed in turns, the processor's side of a frame is 0.50 ms faster at 320 by 180 and not clearly different (−0.13 ms, 95% interval −0.77 to +0.51) at an iPhone's size, and the software renderer's drawing, a stand-in for the graphics chip, is 4.1% slower.

sections.title: What this round set out to do
sections.html:
The request: "Look for low quality assets and increase quality. Make sure it's not too heavy on cpu and gpu."

The previous asset round raised every family of assets by changing colours, normals and shaders only, so that nothing cost more. This round went after what that could not fix: assets whose shapes were too coarse. A finer shape costs triangles, so the round set its budget first and measured against it: draw calls (the processor's cost of each object drawn), triangles and vertices (the graphics chip's cost of shapes, counted in the view and in both shadow maps), textures and their memory, shader programs, and the frame time itself, timed in turns against the previous build.

RequestWhat was doneStatus
Look for low-quality assetsEvery model built in code, the trees, the ground and the props were looked at in fixed views and on their own. Nine kinds of asset stood out as the weakest; they are listed under "The weakest assets" with what was wrong with each.Done
Increase their qualityAll 32 animals and birds rebuilt, with their poses at rest and in flight; the birch, aspen and poplar crowns; the far mountains' rock; the four campfires.Done
Not too heavy on the processor and the graphics chipA budget set before the work: no new draw calls or textures, at most one more shader program, each place's triangles within about 10%. Measured on the final build: draw calls over the eight budget places 1940 before and 1816 after (−6.4%); triangles +4.4% in all, at most +8.6% at one place (Salmon Bend); textures in the materials 87 and 87 (106.27 and 106.27 MB); shader programs 102 and 103. Timed in turns: the processor's side of a frame is 0.50 ms faster at 320 by 180 and not clearly different (−0.13 ms, 95% interval −0.77 to +0.51) at an iPhone's size; the software renderer's drawing, a stand-in for the graphics chip, is 4.1% slower (+79 ms a frame); loading until the game is ready is not clearly different (−108 ms, 95% interval −663 to +447).See Load and Frame time

sections.title: What was found, and why it looked cheap
sections.html:
Found by looking at fixed views of the world, at each animal alone in a fixed light, at each model on a plain sheet, and at the number of triangles of each. What was wrong, and what was done:

AssetWhat was wrongWhat was done
All 32 animals and birdsBuilt from boxes, cylinders and coarse spheres, shaded face by face: 146 to 760 triangles each, legs as plain posts, heads as blocks, no markings beyond a colour per part.Rebuilt as smooth lofted bodies (cross-sections along a spine, so a neck or tail curves without twisting): shaped heads with eyes, ears, muzzles and bills, legs that taper through the joints to hooves, paws and claws, antlers and horns, and markings painted at each vertex (pale bellies, the caribou's white mane, the fox's black stockings, the loon's chequered back). A second, lighter version of every model is drawn while a herd is far off, and every shadow is drawn from it.
Birds at restSwimming ducks, loons and swans showed their open flight wings lying flat on the water; perched eagles, walking cranes and hopping magpies held their wings out too.Wings fold along the body while a bird swims, perches, stands, walks or hops, and a perched or standing bird shows its legs; the open wings appear only in flight.
Birds in flightThe goose, swan, crane, mallard and loon kept their necks upright in flight, as when swimming.In flight the neck swings forward and the head rides on its end, level, as these birds fly; the crane's legs trail behind.
Two species shown wronglyThe game names its gull a glaucous-winged gull and its puffin a tufted puffin; the gull had black wingtips (a glaucous-winged gull's are grey) and the new puffin model was first drawn as a horned puffin (white belly).Grey wingtips on the gull; the puffin all black with a white face, golden tufts, the orange bill and feet.
Animal shadowsShadows were cast by the standing model: a walking moose's shadow did not move its legs, a resting bird's shadow had open wings.One shared shadow material moves the same limbs, so shadows walk, swim and fold their wings with the animal.
Herds out of viewEvery species was drawn every frame, in the view and in both shadow maps, wherever its animals were.Each herd is skipped when a sphere round its animals is out of view (and, for its shadow, out of the shadow map's view).
Birch, aspen and poplar crownsClumps of leaves were 20-sided blocks lit facet by facet, so each crown showed hard flat faces.Close up, each clump is a finer 80-sided ball; further off it keeps its 20 sides but is shaded as a ball. Each clump is lit round inside the crown's own light, with a pattern of leaves taken from a texture already in memory. Vertices are shared, so the crowns are drawn from fewer vertices than before.
The far mountainsBetween 140 and 420 m the rock's crags and gullies are lit by a bump worked out per 2 by 2 block of pixels; on sharp detail the blocks showed as a staircase of light and dark squares on every peak.The crags and gullies are read from blurred levels of their texture, so their light changes smoothly; the rock's grain is put back as colour, and steep cliffs get faint streaks down them.
The four campfiresNine dodecahedron stones and four sticks.A ring of fourteen rounded field stones of mixed sizes and colours, sooted on the side toward the fire, a bed of pale ash with black coals, five split logs leaning together over the fire, charred at the top, and a half-burnt log in the ashes.

sections.title: All 32 animals and birds rebuilt
sections.html:
Every animal and bird is now built from smooth lofted shapes: cross-sections along a spine, framed so that a curving neck or tail does not twist, with rounded or pointed ends. Bodies taper into necks and tails, legs narrow through the knee and hock to hooves, paws and claws, and heads have eyes, ears, muzzles, bills and horns. Markings are painted at each vertex: pale bellies, the moose's dark back, the caribou's white mane, the fox's black stockings, the lynx's ear tufts and spots, the loon's chequered back.

Each species is still one draw call for all its animals (an instanced mesh), and its legs, head, tail and wings still move in the vertex shader. Each model is now indexed: a vertex is stored and shaded once however many triangles meet at it, where the old models repeated it for every triangle. So the new models have about five times the triangles but fewer vertices than before.

Each species also has a far version, built by the same code with fewer points round each cross-section and fewer cross-sections (about 40% of the triangles). A herd is drawn in it while its nearest animal is more than 28 times the model's radius away, where a sphere round the whole animal fills about 6% of the view's height (a moose 55 m off, a wolf 27 m, a hare 7 m), and every shadow map draws every herd in it: a shadow shows only an outline, softened. At that distance the two versions are hard to tell apart (the last picture below).

sections.title: Wings folded at rest, necks out in flight
sections.html:
Birds now have two sets of wings: open wings for flight and wings folded along the body for rest, with the legs of a perched or standing bird. The shader shows one set or the other from what the bird is doing: swimming, perching, standing, walking and hopping birds fold their wings (before, a swimming duck showed its flight wings lying open on the water).

In flight, the five long-necked birds stretch their necks out: the neck swings forward from its base and the head is carried to its end, staying level, so the bill points ahead. The crane trails its legs. As these birds fly: the sandhill crane (All About Birds), the trumpeter swan (All About Birds), the Canada goose (Chesapeake Bay Program); the common loon flies hunchbacked with its head held low (Hinterland Who's Who), which the loon's forward-leaning neck gives too.

Two species now look like the ones the game names in its photo album: the glaucous-winged gull has grey wingtips, a shade darker than its back, not the black ones of most gulls (All About Birds); the tufted puffin is all black with a white face, yellow tufts curling back over the nape, a thick orange bill and orange feet (National Audubon Society).

figs.caption: The twelve birds in their flight pose, as the shader places them: crane, mallard, eagle, goose; gull, kingfisher, loon, magpie; ptarmigan, puffin, raven, swan

sections.title: Birch, aspen and poplar crowns without their facets
sections.html:
A broadleaf crown is a set of clumps. Close up, the birch's and the poplar's clumps are now 80-sided balls instead of 20-sided blocks (the aspen's close clumps had 80 sides already, but were lit facet by facet); further off every clump keeps its 20 sides, which its outline does not show at that distance, but is shaded as a ball. Every clump is lit by its place in the crown (its outside bright, its inside dark) and by its own round shape, and a pattern of leaves is laid over it from the pebble channel of the ground's detail texture, which is already in memory, read in the tree's own frame so it sways with the leaves. The pattern stays off the bark (told apart by its colour, as the bark's shading already was).

The shading depends only on where a vertex is, so the faces that meet at a vertex share it: the crowns are drawn from fewer vertices than before, the close ones from more triangles. The close bands were shortened a little (birch 50 → 45 m, poplar 75 → 66 m) and the poplar's inner clumps, mostly hidden, keep 20 sides.

sections.title: Far rock without the blocky staircase
sections.html:
Between 140 and 420 m, the mountains' rock gets crags and gullies tens of metres across, more than the ground's mesh carries, as a bump: a height read from a texture, lit per pixel by its slope. The slope is worked out once for each 2 by 2 block of pixels (Microsoft, ddx_coarse), so a height that changed sharply within a block lit whole blocks light or dark: a staircase of squares over every far peak.

The crags and gullies are now read from blurred levels of the same texture (a mipmap bias of 3), whose heights change smoothly within a block. The sharp grain the bump lost is put back as colour, which the texture's filtering handles cleanly, and steep rock gets faint streaks down it from the same texture stretched tall. It is the same texture: the crags and gullies are the same two reads as before, and two reads are new: one for the grain, on all ground beyond 140 m, and one for the streaks, wherever the ground is rock.

sections.title: The fifteen fixed views
sections.html:
The fifteen fixed views from tools/scenarios/gfx-views.json, both builds: the same places and hours with the clock stopped, the same random numbers, High quality at 800 by 450, no cloud shadows. Animals and fish move between runs, so the ones in view are not always the same.

Two pictures were taken again. The previous build's night came out moonless in its first run and moonlit when the same view was taken again on the same build, as in the final build's run; the moonlit one is shown, so both sides have the same sky. The final build's Moose Lake at sunset first showed another place in the water: the machine was running four tests at once, no frame was drawn in the three seconds the view waits, and the water's reflection was made from where the camera had been. Taken again it reflects the lake's own shore, and the scenario now also waits for three of the game's frames before it makes the reflection.

The renderer's textures and geometries move by a few between runs of the same build, as things are made when first needed (one run of the previous build held one more texture). The far versions of the animals add 32 small geometries, within that spread. The one more shader program is the shadow material that moves the animals' limbs, shared by every herd. The leaf pattern reads the ground's detail texture, already in memory; the ground's shader reads its rock texture twice more (the grain on ground beyond 140 m, the streaks on rock). The game's file grows by the code that builds the new models; the models themselves are built when the game starts, as before.

sections.title: Timed in turns against the previous build
sections.html:
The frame-time tour of both builds in turns with tools/perf-compare.mjs: 6 rounds of each comparison, each build first in half of them, every run a fresh browser and the whole tour: five stretches of 90 frames each (turning on the spot at Hotrod Landing in the afternoon, a walk in the forest, a drive along a road, Bear Falls with the Tesla memorial, and the observatory at night). Each run's average is fitted on its round, its place in the round and its build, and a difference counts only when its 95% interval leaves out zero.

The first two rows time the processor's side of each frame: the game's update and the renderer issuing its draw calls. The third has each frame really drawn by the test machine's software renderer, which does the graphics chip's work (vertices and pixels) on the processor: a rough stand-in for a graphics chip's load, not for its speed. It takes about 2 seconds a frame, so its tour has 16 frames a stretch instead of 90 (a tour of 90 could not finish inside the 15 minutes the tool allows it).

Processor's side, 320 by 1808.227.71−0.50 (−0.92 to −0.08)faster

The drawing, stretch by stretch

The software renderer's time in each stretch of the drawn tour, averaged over the six runs of each build, with the triangles of a frame in the middle of the stretch. The extra time is spread over every stretch, the observatory at night among them, where the frame has fewer triangles than before. So at least part of it is work done for each pixel rather than for each triangle, most likely the new texture reads (the leaf pattern on the broadleaf crowns, the grain on far ground and the streaks on rock). Switching each read off in turn at the observatory changed the drawing by less than the machine itself drifted while it was measured (175 ms between two measurements of the unchanged shaders, of about 2 300), so no one read stands out.

sections.title: What the audit found, and what was fixed
sections.html:
Every shader built, without an error

A development build checks each shader program as it is first used. Both builds were loaded, everything in the world and the hands compiled and drawn once at High, Medium and Low in turn, and frames drawn at morning, sunset, night, noon and in rain (tools/shader-check.mjs): 254 programs before with 0 failing, 255 after with 0 failing (the one more is the animals' shadow material). The browser printed 95 and 1 errors or warnings: in both runs, that the software renderer cannot compile shaders in parallel; in the previous build's run also the warm-up draws it rejected. The browser does not print every such warning: read directly after every draw, the final build has the same rejected draws as the previous one (below).

With tools/gl-errors.mjs (the same steps, with the browser's error read after every draw): the draws it rejects are the same in both builds, and only in the warm-up draw the game makes once at load, before any shadow map exists: the water reflection's ground and trees and the far ground, drawn in the view instead of in the reflection, with an empty texture where their shadow sampler expects a depth texture. Every one of these meshes is drawn correctly in the frames after it; the warm-up still compiles their programs. It was there before this round.

The independent code review

A separate review of the whole change looked for defects that would break drawing, animation, shadows, culling, hunting, memory or the tools, and verified each finding against the code before reporting it.

FindingSeverityWhat was done
The whale's and the orca's flukes and flippers were mirrored with a half turn, which does not mirror a part: one fluke pointed straight back and the other forward through the tail stock, the orca's second fluke poked out of its right flank, and the right flipper was raised and swept forward.Visible defect, new in this roundMirrored with a scale of −1 across the body instead. Checked in numbers (the two flukes now span the same distance to either side and sweep back by the same amount) and on the model sheet.
The fish an eagle steals hung 0.58 m below its belly instead of 0.24 m: the eagle's origin moved from its body to its feet, so it could stand on a perch, and the fish was still placed 0.4 m below the origin.Cosmetic, new in this roundThe fish is placed 0.34 m higher, in the talons just under the belly.

The review also checked, and found correct: every shader text the change inserts against three.js r186's own shader pieces (the Lambert and depth shaders); that no two shader variants share one compiled program by mistake; the one shadow material shared by every herd; the culling sphere against sampled poses of all 32 models (legs, heads, tails, wings and necks at their widest swing); that every model stays under 65 536 vertices and carries every attribute the shader reads; the limb numbers and pivots; the hunting hit zones of all seven species that can be hunted (within about 0.1 m of the old models); that nothing still treats the new models or crowns as unindexed; the flap values every bird state sends; the terrain shader on every quality level; the leaf pattern's names against the other patches on the same material; the campfire's colours; and the timing tools' new option.

What the pictures and the measurements showed

FoundWhat was done
The gull had black wingtips; the game names it a glaucous-winged gull, whose wingtips are grey like its back.The wingtips are now a shade darker than the grey back, as the species' are.
The first new puffin was a horned puffin (white belly); the game names it a tufted puffin.Rebuilt as a tufted puffin: all black, a white face, golden tufts curling back from behind the eyes, the orange bill and orange feet.
In flight the goose, swan, crane, mallard and loon kept their necks upright, as when swimming.The neck now swings forward in flight and the head rides on its end, level (two new limb kinds in the shader); the crane trails its legs.
The campfire's ash bed read as a blue disc: a near-black surface lit mostly by the blue sky.Pale wood-ash grey, with black coals on it and soot on the stones' inner faces.
The first change to the crowns (each facet lit a little less sharply) was a small improvement only.Finer clumps close up, each clump shaded round inside the crown's light, and a leaf pattern.
The first complete build put each frame's triangles up by 7 to 28% at the eight budget places, against a budget of about 10%: the new animals were drawn at full detail however far off, and so were their shadows, and the finer crowns ran out to 180 m.A lighter version of every animal for herds far off, every shadow drawn from it, the finer crowns only in the closest band (birch to 45 m, poplar to 66 m) with the poplar's inner clumps coarse, and coarse clumps shaded round beyond. Measured again in the Load section.
The final build's first picture of Moose Lake at sunset showed another place in the water.Not the game, the test: with four tests running at once no frame was drawn in the three seconds the view waits, so the water's reflection was made from where the camera had been. Three more runs read where each reflection was made: in the one that went wrong it was the last place, and the reflection was right after the next frames. The views scenario now waits for three of the game's frames as well.
The shader check of the previous build showed the browser rejecting some draws (a texture of the wrong kind for its sampler).Found with a new tool, tools/gl-errors.mjs: only the game's warm-up draw at load, which draws the water reflection's ground and trees once before any shadow map exists. It was there before this round and nothing is drawn wrongly because of it; see the shader check.
The drawn timing, with the software renderer drawing every frame, could not finish: at about two seconds a frame, a tour of 90 frames a stretch ran past the 15 minutes the timing tool allows each tour.Timed again with 16 frames a stretch, after one short tour of each build had measured how long a frame takes; see Frame time.
The README gave the game's file as 1.9 MB (690 KB compressed), out of date since the recorded voice was packed in.Corrected to 3.0 MB (about 1.3 MB compressed); this round adds 40 KB of it (see Load).

sections.title: What this report cannot show
sections.html:
• No real iPhone or iPad was used. The pictures and the timings come from Chromium drawing in software on the test machine. The shapes and colours are the same on any device; how an iPhone's graphics chip handles the extra triangles and texture reads was not measured.
  • The software renderer's drawing time stands in for a graphics chip's load, not its speed. An iPhone's graphics chip first sorts every triangle of a frame into small tiles of the screen and only then shades them (Apple), so its cost per triangle and per pixel differs from a processor's.
  • The counts move between runs. Animals walk and fly, and the reflection's ground streams in at its own pace, so one place's triangles varied by up to 47 thousand between runs of the previous build and 41 thousand between runs of the final one. The means of several runs and the total over eight places are steadier than any one number.
  • A herd is drawn near or far as a whole. While any one of its animals is close, the whole herd is drawn in near detail; a big herd or flock round the player costs more than the eight places show. The worst case is the caribou's herd of up to 20 at 3 204 triangles each in view.
  • The smallest difference the timings could see is about 0.42 ms a frame at 320 by 180, 0.64 ms at an iPhone's size and 76 ms in the software renderer, and about 555 ms in the loading time: the half-widths of the 95% intervals. A smaller cost could still be there.
  • Each species was pictured once in the lineup, in one pose and light; the model sheets show every model from one more side. A fault seen only from another side, or only in motion, would not show here.
  • Sources were read through web search. curl is blocked for every host in this environment, so the pages below were found and summarised by search, not downloaded in full. To allow hosts: the cloud environment menu in the session's title bar, then Edit, then Network access (a broader level, or Custom with the hosts added under Allowed domains); the steps are at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cloud-environments#network-access.

sections.title: What would change this conclusion
sections.html:
The conclusion: the weakest assets look much better for a small, measured cost, all of it on the graphics chip's side: about 4% more drawing time in the software renderer, while the processor's side of a frame is no slower. Over the eight budget places the frame draws 1816 calls where it drew 1940, and 4.4% more triangles (at most 8.6% more at one place), with the same 87 textures in the materials and one more shader program (102 → 103). Timed in turns, the processor's side of a frame is 0.50 ms faster at 320 by 180 and not clearly different (−0.13 ms, 95% interval −0.77 to +0.51) at an iPhone's size, the software renderer's drawing is 4.1% slower (+79 ms a frame), and loading is not clearly different (−108 ms, 95% interval −663 to +447). This would change if:

  • An iPhone's graphics chip finds the new work heavier than measured here. The new work is the extra triangles and three new texture reads: one for every pixel of a close or middle-distance birch, aspen or poplar (the leaf pattern), one for every pixel of ground beyond 140 m (the grain) and one for every pixel of rock (the streaks), which cost most where far mountains fill the view. The test that would settle it is the two builds taking turns on the same iPhone, timed with Safari's Web Inspector on its frame timeline, at Salmon Bend and in the forest, where the crowns add most, and at the glacier, where rock fills the view.
  • Players spend their time beside big herds and flocks. A herd with one animal close is drawn in near detail entirely; if that shows in the frame time, the next step is a near and a far copy of each herd, which costs a draw call more for a species seen both near and far.
  • The switch from near to far detail is seen. It happens where a sphere round the whole animal fills about 6% of the view's height. Pictured still at that distance, the two versions are hard to tell apart (the last picture under Animals and birds): between 2 and 42 of the 1 536 pixels in a box round each animal's middle change by more than a tenth of their brightness. In motion a switch could still catch the eye; if it does, the distance can be raised, at a cost in triangles.
  • The new crowns or animals look wrong in a light the views do not show. The fifteen views cover morning, noon, evening, sunset and night, and the regression scenarios add close looks at the trees, the animals, the hunt and the bear; a dusk under heavy cloud was not pictured.
